blocks.text: The Stage represents a dark, subterraneous dungeon; on the left of the spectators is an old reservoir covered with stones and rubbish. In the background are several openings provided with gratings in the wall, through which a staircase is seen, leading down from above; on the right, the lower steps, and the door in the prison. A lamp is burning, Florestan alone, he is sitting upon a stone, a long chain round his waist, the end of which is fastened in the wall.

lines: Oh, heavens, what dreary gloom! what awful stillness this!
All is desert around, naught breathes life but me,
Oh! heavy trial! but let the will of God be done.
I do not murmur; thou knowest when the cup of sorrow is full.
In the days of my spring, happiness, all happiness has fled.
Truth I boldly spoke, and chains are my reward;
These sufferings I bear willingly, and die with resignation;
Sweet solace feels this heart my duty I fulfilled!

blocks.text: In a state of inspiration but with calmness.

lines: Do I not hear soft murmurs in the air?
Does not a ray of light surround my grave?
Yes, I behold, in roseate vapor clad, a beauteous angel like my Leonora,
Stand by my side, to point me out the way to liberty and to celestial bliss!

blocks.text: He sinks exhausted by his last agitation, upon the rocky seat; his hands cover his face.

Rocquo, Leonora, Florestan. The two former, who are seen through the aperture by the light of a lantern, carry a pitcher and the tools for digging. The back door opens and the stage becomes half lighted.
How cold it is in this subterraneous cave!
That’s natural, it being so deep.
looking anxiously around on all sides
I thought already we should not find the entrance.
half loud, endeavoring to recognize the prisoner
No, no, he only sleeps. Let us take advantage of that and proceed to work, we have no time to lose.
It is impossible to distinguish his features, but; oh heavens assist if it is him!
Here, below this rubbish is the old cistern, of which I told you. It will not take us long to get at the opening. Give me your pick-ax, and come here. You tremble. Are you afraid?
Oh no, it is only so cold.
Well, then, go on; you will soon get warm with your work.
During the symphony, Leonora takes advantage of the moment when Rocquo stoops to observe the prisoner. The Duett is sung throughout in an undertone.
Only get on quickly, and with smart digging; before long he will come down.
You shall not have to complain; for to me no labor is too hard.
lifting up a large stone on the spot where he went down
Come—Help me to lift this stone. Take care; take care; it is very heavy.
I’ll help you directly. Never fear; I’ll exert myself to the utmost.
They roll the stone over the rubbish, and take breath. Rocquo sets to work again.
Only get on quickly, and with good smart digging. He will soon be here.
Let me only gain breath again.
Observes the prisoner, whilst Rocquo, turned away from her, works with his back bent.
Who ever thou art, I will save thee. By all that’s sacred, thou shalt not fall a sacrifice! For certain I will loose thy chain: I will set thee free, thou poor wretched man.
What, are you at your work?
No, father, no! I do not hesitate.
Only get on quickly, and with good smart digging. He will soon be here.
You shall not complain; for no toil is hard to me.
Florestan recovers himself, and raises his head up, without turning towards Leonora.
still looking towards Florestan, in the greatest agitation
Yes—he has just raised up his head.
Doubtless, he will put me again a thousand questions; I must speak alone with him. He will soon, now, have overcome it all.
He comes out of the grave.
Do you go down, instead of me; and clear away as much as you can, so that we may open the cistern.
She goes a few steps down, tremblingly
What passes within me is unspeakable.
Now you have reposed again a little?
How could I possibly find repose?
That voice! If I could but see his face for an instant—
Will you always be deaf to my complaints? cruel man.
With the last words, he turns his face towards Leonora.
God of Heaven! It is him.
She falls senseless on the edge of the grave.
What do you require of me, then? I fulfill the orders given to me;—that is my province, my duty.
Only tell me then—at once—who is the governor of this prison.
Now I can tell him well enough, without danger.
The governor of this prison is Don Pizzarro.
Oh, barbarian! Thy cruelty—thy very name restores me to my strength.
Oh! send—send—as quickly as possible to Seville. Ask there for Leonora Florestan.
Lord of mercy! He suspects not that she is now digging his grave.
Tell her that I am lying here in chains.
It is impossible, I tell you, I should be ruining myself, without doing you any benefit.
If, then, I am condemned to pine away here, Oh! let me not so slowly linger to my end.
springs up, and then restrains herself
Oh God! Who can endure this?
For pity’s sake, give me only a drop of water;—surely that is little enough.
It goes against my very heart.
I cannot procure you what you request. All that I can offer you is a remnant of wine, which I have in the pitcher.
bringing the pitcher with the utmost haste
There it is; there it is.
My assistant;—and in a few days, my son-in-law.
Hands the pitcher to Florestan, who drinks.
There is, truly not much wine; yet I am glad to give it you.
Who could help being so? You, yourself, Mr. Rocquo—
It is true—the man has such a voice—
Yes;—it penetrates to the inmost recesses of the heart.
May you find a reward in the next world. Heaven has sent you to me. Oh, thanks! you have sweetly revived me. I cannot reward thy kindness.
Heaven send thee deliverance; then will I be highly rewarded.
Your sufferings often moved me; but to keep you was strictly forbidden me.
Softly to Leonora, whom he takes aside.
I was glad, Heaven knows, to refresh the poor man. But it is already all over with him. I do what my duty imposes, yet I abhor all cruelty.
How my heart is beating; my life fluctuates between joy and grief. The awful hour beckons on, that death or deliverance does bring.
I see this youth here affected; and this man also shows compassion. O God! thou sendest me hope, that I may again find her for whom alone I live.
softly to Rocquo, while she draws a small piece of bread out of her pocket
This piece of bread I have carried about me for the last two days.
I would most willingly; but I tell you that would indeed be venturing too much.
You like to refresh the poor man.
That will not do; that will not do.
It will very soon be all over with him.
So be it then; you may venture it.
in the greatest agitation, handing Florestan the bread
There, take the bread, poor man.
Yes, it will be very soon all over with him.
grasping Leonora’s hand, and pressing it to himself.
Oh, thank ye! thank ye! be your reward heavenly bliss!
Oh, more than I can endure.
It will soon be over with him.
Oh, that I cannot reward you.
He eats the piece of bread.
after a momentary silence, to Leonora
All is ready. I am going to give the signal.
to Leonora, while Rocquo goes to open the door
Rocquo opens the door, and gives the signal by a loud whistle.
Is that the harbinger of my death?
No, no, calm yourself, dear prisoner.
Oh, my Leonora! shall I never then see thee again?
She seems to feel herself drawn towards Florestan, and strives to overcome the impulse
My whole heart draws me to him.
Be composed I tell you. Do not forget whatever you may hear and see—do not forget that there is a Providence above.
She separates from him, and goes towards the cistern.
Enter Pizzarro, disguised in a mantle.
to Rocquo, in a feigned voice
Yes; the cistern has only to be opened.
Good. The lad must go away.
Must I not take the irons from the prisoner? Go, go!
Leonora withdraws to the background, and approaches gradually again in the shade towards Florestan, her eyes directed constantly to the person in the disguise.
aside, casting a look at Rocquo and Leonora
To-day I must shake off from me these two, that all may for ever remain in silence.
Shall I take off his chains?
He dies; but he shall first know who it is that pierces his proud heart. Let the darkness be torn away that veils revenge. Behold! thou hast not deceived thyself!
Pizzarro, whom thou wishedst to overthrow!—Pizzarro, whom thou should’st fear to look upon, stands now before thee, his own avenger!
Yet, for once will I recall thee to what thou hast done; yet one moment, and my dagger—
springs forward with a piercing shriek, and covers Florestan with her body.
Thou must first stab through this breast. Death is sworn to thee for thy blood-thirstiness!
Oh, yes, yes, see here your Leonora!
I am his wife. I have sworn aid to him, destruction to thee.
His wife! What unheard of courage!
My heart will burst with joy!
My blood runs cold with terror!
Shall I tremble before a woman? No! I will sacrifice them both to my rage. Thou hast shared life with him,—now then partake his doom in death.
He is about to assail her, when Leonora suddenly draws a small pistol out of her bosom, and holds it before Pizzarro.
Another word, and you are dead!
The trumpet is heard from the tower.
Ha! the minister! Hell and death!
Oh, what is that? Just heaven!
Pizzarro stands confounded. Rocquo the same. Leonora hangs on Florestan’s neck. The trumpet sounds louder.
Jacquino, two officers, and soldiers, with torches, appear at the uppermost grated opening of the gates.
speaks during the pause of the music
Father Rocquo, the minister arrives; his guard is already before the castle gate.
We are coming! yes, we are coming immediately; and the men with their torches shall come down and accompany the Governor up.
The soldiers come down as far as the door. The Officers and Jacquino go out again.
Curst be this evil hour! Hell mocks at me! Despair now leagues itself with my revenge!
Dread suspense! Oh! what fresh affliction is now in store for me? I will no longer be controlled by this tyrant. The moment of vengeance is come; thou shalt be free!
The moment of vengeance is come; thou shalt be free! Love, in league with courage, will still make me free.

Pizzarro hastens away, giving Rocquo a sign to follow him. He avails himself of the moment when Pizzarro is going and unites the hands of the husband and wife, presses them to his bosom, points toward heaven, and follows him. The soldiers light Pizzarro off.
Faithful wife! what hast thou suffered for me!

lines: Oh, joy unknown! My husband again restored to my fond embrace!
Pressed to my Leonora’s breast, after great sufferings! Oh, delight past utterance!

blocks.text: Good news! My poor sufferers! The minister has a list of all the prisoners. You are all to be brought before him.
You alone are not mentioned. Your detention here is an arbitrary action on the part of the governor himself. Come, follow me! follow me up.

The castle guard march up; then the minister Don Fernando, accompanied by Pizzarro and Officers on one side. People assemble as spectators; and on the other side appear, accompanied by Jacquino and Marceline the state prisoners. They all throw themselves on their knees before Don Fernando. Afterwards Rocquo, with Florestan and Leonora, press through the people and through the guard.
All hail the day! All hail the hour, long sought for yet unhoped! Justice, united with mercy, appears to us on the shrine of death.
The command and wish of the best of kings brings me to you, poor wearied sufferers! that I unveil crimes and dreary sorrows, which surround you deep and full. No longer kneel down slavishly.
The tyrant’s power I cherish not. A brother loving I come, and help where help can be.
Enter Rocquo, conducting Leonora and Florestan.
There, there,—Help here! help the poor captive.
For mercy sake, have pity, and reunite this hapless pair.
He that was supposed dead? The hero, who fought for truth and right?
And who has suffered torments unimaginable.
My friend! supposed dead;—how is this, that chained, pallid, and exhausted, he stands before me?
Yes,—it is Florestan! you see him here.
I present the pride, the ornament of her sex. She came hither—
There, at my gate;—she entered my service as a hireling boy, and served me so well and faithfully, that I chose her for a son-in-law.
Oh, woe is me!—What meets my ear!
Within this very hour, the cruel man would do a deed of murder on Florestan.
Yes, my lord, he wanted us to join in his base design. Your arrival only drove him away.

lines: Punishment be to the villain who oppress the innocent!
Justice hold for judgment the drawn sword of revenge.

blocks.text: Thou liftedst the grave that threatened this noble heart,—now take off his chains;—yet stay,—You noble woman! to you alone it becomes completely to set him free!
takes the keys, loosens the chains from off Florestan, with great agitation. He sinks into Leonora’s arms.
Just, O heaven, are thy judgments!
Thou triest—but thou dost not forsake us.
Whoever has obtained such a partner of his heart, let him join in our jubilee. Who can ever sufficiently praise the wife that frees her husband from his chains!
Your fidelity my life restores. Virtue is the sinner’s dread.
Love guided my endeavors; true love knows no fear.
Let us sing praises high to the noble strife of Leonora.
Whoever has obtained a wife, etc.
Guided by love, my success is complete. Your chains are broken! high praise be to love; my Florestan again I embrace.
